summary: This unit teaches you to conduct a systems evaluation in a Jamaican public body or business: to define the purpose and scope, write terms of reference, choose evaluation questions and criteria, build a logic model, collect and analyse data fairly and ethically, turn findings into specific recommendations, report to senior managers and staff, and make sure the changes are carried out and checked.

blocks.p: A **system** is a set of linked people, rules, forms, equipment and steps that produce a result: for example a way of processing staff leave, collecting fees, licensing vendors or booking clinic appointments. A **systems evaluation** is a planned, evidence-based judgement of how well a system works and how it can be improved. It is different from monitoring, which is the routine checking of progress, and from an audit, which mainly checks compliance with rules.

This unit is for Level 5 managers and senior officers in ministries, agencies, municipal corporations, schools and businesses who are asked to review a system and advise leadership. The skills are those of a good investigator: ask the right questions, gather evidence from more than one source, treat people fairly, work out the numbers correctly and write clear, usable recommendations.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your work
rows: Define purpose, scope and boundaries; identify stakeholders; write terms of reference and a timeline.
Write clear evaluation questions and use the criteria of relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, economy, equity and sustainability.
Show how the system should work
Draw a logic model of inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes, and set indicators and a baseline.
Choose records, surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation and process maps; sample fairly; design and test tools.
Be independent, keep confidences, protect personal data and be open about limits.
Work out percentages, averages, cost per case, error rates, payback and gaps; find themes and root causes; compare with standards and similar bodies.
Write findings, conclusions and recommendations; present to leaders and staff; secure a management response and action plan; check results later.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper with scenario questions on planning, criteria, methods, analysis, ethics and reporting.
A written paper with short answers (terms such as baseline, triangulation, logic model, and simple sums) and longer answers in which you plan an evaluation or interpret figures.
Group practicals: planning an evaluation (terms of reference, logic model, evaluation matrix, tools) and analysing a data pack to present findings and recommendations.

blocks.note: Many questions ask for a sum. Write the formula first, then the figures, then check the answer a second time.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Evaluations are done to judge **how well a system works and how to improve it**, to account for public money, to decide whether to continue, change or stop a system, and to learn for the future. Be clear at the start which of these is the main purpose; it shapes everything that follows.

head: Type
Question it answers
When
rows: How can we improve it as it runs?
How well did it do overall?
At the end or after a set period
Is the system being run as designed (forms used, steps followed, time limits met)?
Did it achieve the intended results?
What lasting difference did it make, beyond the system itself?
Is it good value for the money spent?

blocks.p: Before anything else, define **scope, aims and boundaries**: which system, which offices, which time period, and which parts are included. For example, a ministry's staff travel-claims system might be evaluated from claim submission to payment, in the headquarters only, for the last financial year. Without a clear boundary, an evaluation grows endlessly or misses its target.

**Stakeholders** are people and groups affected by the system or with an interest in the evaluation: service users, front-line staff, supervisors, senior managers, finance and legal units, the Permanent Secretary or Chief Executive Officer, suppliers and sometimes the public. Identify them early so that **users' and staff views are included**, and decide who must be consulted, who must approve and who must be informed.
The **terms of reference (ToR)** are the written agreement that sets out what the evaluation will do. A good ToR contains:

ul: **Purpose** and the decisions the evaluation will inform
**Scope** and boundaries (what is in and out)
The **evaluation questions** and the criteria
**Methods** and data sources
The **team**, roles and who is independent
**Governance:** who approves, who is on the steering group, who receives the report
**Ethics:** confidentiality and data protection
**Timeline** and **budget**, with the date of the final report
The **form of the report** and how results will be shared

blocks.note: The ToR is the contract. If the scope changes during the work, change the ToR in writing and have it agreed.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Agree why the evaluation is needed and who will use the results
Define scope, aims and boundaries
Identify stakeholders and form a steering group
Draft evaluation questions and choose criteria
Draw the logic model and set indicators and baseline
Choose methods, sample and tools, and test them
Write the terms of reference, budget and timeline, and get approval

head: Aspect
Internal evaluator
External evaluator
rows: Knows the organisation; cheaper; quick to start
Independent and credible; fresh view; specialist skills
May not be seen as independent; may have loyalties or blind spots
Costs more; needs time to learn the system
Learning and improvement are the main aims
Independence and credibility matter most, for example after public criticism

blocks.p: The person who **designed or runs** a system should not be its sole evaluator: findings may not be seen as independent. Where an internal team is used, add outside review.

A **Gantt chart** is a bar chart that shows each task, who does it and when. It is the best tool for showing the evaluation's tasks and timeline to the steering group. Allow time for approval, data collection, analysis, drafting, comment by stakeholders and the final report.

sections.title: Evaluation questions, criteria and the logic model

blocks.p: Evaluation questions turn the purpose into specific enquiries. A good question is clear, answerable with evidence and linked to a decision. Compare:

head: Weak question
Better question
rows: "Are staff leave requests processed accurately, within five working days and at reasonable cost?"
"How satisfied are service users with the speed and clarity of the process, and what do they find difficult?"
"Does the system achieve its aim of ensuring staff leave balances are correct?"

head: Criterion
Question it asks
Example
rows: Do the system's objectives still match the needs it is meant to serve?
Is a paper booking system still right when most clients use mobile phones?
Does it achieve its intended results?
Are the clients who apply actually receiving their licences?
How well does it turn inputs into outputs (time or cost per case)?
Cost per case; cases per staff member
Were inputs (equipment, staff, supplies) obtained at the lowest cost for the quality required?
Did procurement of terminals obtain fair prices?
Does it serve all groups fairly, including those who find it harder to use?
An online-only system that older rural clients struggle to use
Will it keep working and its benefits last once project funds end?
Can the agency run it from its own budget and skills?

blocks.note: Do not confuse efficiency with economy. Economy is about the **price of inputs**; efficiency is about **how well inputs are turned into outputs**; effectiveness is about **whether the intended results are achieved**.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **logic model** is a diagram that links a system's inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes. It shows how the system is supposed to work, so that you can test each link.

head: Element
Meaning
Example: a youth skills programme
rows: Share of graduates in jobs after six months
Lower youth unemployment in the parish

blocks.p: Distinguish **outputs** (what is produced) from **outcomes** (what changes as a result). "Number of certificates issued" is an output; "share of graduates in work after six months" is an outcome.

ul: An **indicator** is a measurable sign of progress, for example "the share of applications completed within the target time".
A **baseline** is the measurement of an indicator before a change or at the start, used as the starting point for comparison. Without it, you cannot say whether a system has improved.
Each indicator needs a source of data, a collection date and an owner.
Use a few indicators that matter; too many drown the evaluation.

blocks.p: An **evaluation matrix** is a table that links each evaluation question to its indicators, data sources, methods and who collects it. Use it to check that every question is covered by at least two sources of evidence and that you do not collect data nobody needs.

head: Question
Indicator
Data source
Method
rows: Do staff find it easy to use?

head: Method
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Records may be incomplete or inconsistent
Views of many users, quickly and at low cost
Low response rate; poor question design
Group views and how people react to each other
A few people may dominate; confidentiality
What actually happens at the counter or on the system
People may act differently when watched
Each step and handover; where delays arise
Must be checked with the people who do the work

blocks.p: A survey tells you **how many** think something; interviews tell you **why**. Use in-depth interviews rather than a large survey when you need to understand reasons.

**Triangulation** is using several sources or methods to check that findings agree. If system data shows complaints answered in five days on average, but users say they wait for weeks, do not choose one; **check other sources, such as files**, to find out. A fact supported by two or three independent sources can be relied on with more confidence.

When you cannot check every case, take a **sample**. A fair sample is chosen so that every case has an equal chance of selection (**random sampling**), for example by numbering the cases in the list and using random numbers. A **proportional (stratified) sample** takes the right share from each group.

Worked example: a records unit has 1,500 files, of which 900 are from Kingston and 600 from rural offices. A proportional sample of 75 files should include 600 ÷ 1,500 = 40% rural files: 0.4 × 75 = **30** rural and 45 Kingston files.

blocks.note: A sample of the easiest files, or the files the supervisor suggests, is not fair. Choose them at random from the full list.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Keep it short, with clear plain questions, in the language users prefer.
Ask one thing at a time.
Avoid **leading questions** that push the answer, such as "Don't you agree the new system is much better?" Ask instead: "How would you rate the new system?"
Include a mix of rating questions and a few open questions.
**Test it with a few users** first (a pilot), to find unclear questions and fix them.
Explain the purpose, say that replies are confidential and that taking part is voluntary.

blocks.p: The **response rate** is the share of people asked who actually reply: replies ÷ people asked × 100. For example, 144 replies from 400 people is 36%. A low response rate means the results may not represent all users, and the report must say so.

head: Principle
What it means in practice
rows: Do not evaluate a system you designed; declare any conflict of interest; report what the evidence shows, even if it is unwelcome
If staff were promised confidentiality, report their comments as themes, without identifying anyone
Explain the purpose and use of the information; allow people to decline
Use personal information, such as names and addresses, only as agreed, and keep it secure; share only what is needed
State the limits of the data and method
Treat all participants courteously, including those who are fearful or angry

blocks.p: If **staff fear that an evaluation will be used to cut jobs** and refuse to take part, explain its purpose and how the findings will be used. Honesty and clear commitments build trust; false promises destroy it.

head: Measure
How to work it out
Worked example
rows: Average time falls from 30 to 24 days: 6 ÷ 30 = 20% reduction
Cost of change ÷ saving per year

blocks.p: Always compare a result with its **target** and with the **baseline**. For example, a target of 90% of applications completed within 10 days and an actual 1,620 of 1,800 completed (90%) means the target was met exactly; 1,530 of 1,800 would be 85%, so the target was missed.

Do not compare totals; compare **rates**. Suppose Office A spends J$7,200,000 to process 1,800 cases and Office B spends J$6,300,000 to process 1,260 cases. Cost per case: A = J$4,000; B = J$5,000. Office A is cheaper per case even though it spent more in total. But a fair comparison also asks about quality (error rates, share on time), and whether the cases are of the same type.

flow: Read all the comments once
Group similar comments into themes (for example "long waits", "unclear forms", "helpful staff")
Count how often each theme appears
Choose short typical quotes, without names
Report the main themes with their frequency, and note the minority views

blocks.p: When something goes wrong, ask why until you reach a cause that can be fixed, and test each suspected cause against the data.

head: Tool
How it works
Example
rows: Ask why of each answer, usually up to five times
Applications returned as incomplete: why? The form is unclear; why? It has not been revised for years; why? No one owns the form
A diagram, shaped like a fish skeleton, with the problem at the head and causes grouped on the bones: people, methods, equipment, materials, environment
Delays in payment grouped under staff, procedures, IT system, forms
Finds a step where files wait three days for a signature

ul: A **gap analysis** compares current performance with the standard or target, to see the size of the gap and where it lies.
**Benchmarking** compares performance with that of similar organisations or with best practice, to see what good performance looks like.
Make sure comparisons are like for like: similar size, type of work and period.

head: Chart
Best for
rows: How a measure changed over time, such as monthly processing times over two years
Showing parts of a whole, with few categories

blocks.p: Evaluators often mix these three. Keep them apart.

head: Step
What it is
Example
rows: 25% of claims were returned for missing receipts
A judgement drawn from findings and criteria
The system is not efficient: one in four claims needs rework
A specific action that follows from the conclusion
Redesign the form to list required receipts, and test it with staff by 31 March

ul: **Specific:** what exactly is to be done
**Actionable:** within the power of the people addressed
**Owner and date:** who will do it and by when
**Linked to evidence:** it follows from a finding
**Realistic:** with cost and benefit considered (for example by working out the payback period)
**Few and prioritised:** a long list of vague actions is rarely followed

head: Vague
Specific
rows: "Train all counter staff on the new system by 31 March, and check by observation in April."
"Send a weekly status report on delayed claims to unit heads, starting 15 February."

blocks.p: If a manager asks you to remove a critical finding that is supported by evidence, **keep it and offer to discuss the evidence**. You may correct a factual error or soften unfair wording, but you must not remove a well-supported finding. If serious weaknesses are found, brief the unit's staff **factually, focusing on the system**, not on blaming individuals.

flow: Title page, contents and list of abbreviations
Executive summary: the key findings and recommendations, briefly (one page)
Background, purpose, scope and the evaluation questions
Methods, with the sample sizes and the response rate
Findings, organised by question or criterion, with charts and tables
Conclusions
Recommendations, with owners and dates
Limitations
Annexes: tools, data tables and the terms of reference

blocks.p: The **executive summary** is for the senior reader who may read nothing else. Put the key findings and recommendations there, briefly and in plain language.
State the **limitations**, such as a low survey response, missing records or a short time. This lets readers judge how far to rely on the findings. Hiding limits damages trust in the whole report.

ul: To senior management: a short briefing with the main findings, the recommendations and the decisions needed.
To the staff who run the system: a factual session showing the findings fairly, thanking those who helped, and discussing practical solutions.
Use charts for trends and comparisons, and keep slides plain.
Check every figure twice before presenting.

flow: Management reads the report and meets the evaluators to discuss it
Management prepares a **management response**: which recommendations it accepts, which it does not and why
An **action plan** is agreed with owners, dates and resources
Progress is tracked at regular intervals by a named person
After a set time (for example six months), the **agreed indicators** are measured again and compared with the **baseline**
Results are reported and lessons shared

blocks.note: In public bodies, the report normally goes to the Permanent Secretary, Chief Executive Officer or board. Follow the agency's rules on who may see it and on classification. Do not release personal information, and follow the access to information and data protection laws.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: After an evaluation report is accepted, management should produce a **response and action plan with owners and dates**. Six months later, track the agreed indicators against the baseline to see whether the changes made a difference. Without follow-up, evaluation is wasted effort.

ul: explain what a systems evaluation is and distinguish it from monitoring and audit.
distinguish formative, summative, process, outcome and impact evaluations.
define scope and boundaries and identify stakeholders.
write terms of reference with all the necessary parts.
weigh the use of internal and external evaluators.
write clear evaluation questions and apply relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, economy, equity and sustainability.
draw a logic model and tell outputs from outcomes.
set indicators and a baseline and build an evaluation matrix.
choose records, surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation and process maps, and triangulate.
take a random or proportional sample and design a fair questionnaire.
act with independence, confidentiality and care for personal data.
work out cost per case, percentage change, error rate, response rate, payback and share within target.
group comments into themes and find root causes with "why" questions and a fishbone diagram.
write findings, conclusions and specific recommendations with owners and dates.
structure a report, state its limitations and present to leaders and staff.
secure a management response and action plan and check results against the baseline.

terms: Systems evaluation
A planned, evidence-based judgement of how well a system works and how to improve it.
Terms of reference
The document that sets out an evaluation's purpose, scope, questions, methods and timeline.
Stakeholder
A person or group affected by the system or interested in the evaluation.
Formative evaluation
An evaluation carried out while a system is running, to improve it.
Summative evaluation
An evaluation carried out at the end, to judge overall results.
Logic model
A diagram linking inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes.
Baseline
The measure of performance before a change, used as the starting point for comparison.
Indicator
A measurable sign of progress or performance.
Relevance
Whether a system's objectives still match the needs it serves.
Effectiveness
Whether the system achieves its intended results.
Efficiency
How well inputs are turned into outputs, for example cost or time per case.
Economy
Obtaining inputs at the lowest cost for the quality required.
Equity
Fair service to all groups, including those who find access harder.
Sustainability
Whether benefits last once project funds end.
Triangulation
Using several sources or methods to check that findings agree.
Response rate
The share of people asked to complete a survey who actually do so.
Benchmarking
Comparing performance with similar organisations or with best practice.
Fishbone diagram
A diagram, shaped like a fish skeleton, showing possible causes of a problem.
Management response
Managers' formal written reply to an evaluation, stating which recommendations they accept and what they will do.

c1.title: Evaluating a ministry's staff leave system
c1.text: A ministry in Kingston has 1,200 staff and a paper-and-email system for approving leave. Staff complain that leave balances are wrong and approvals are slow. The Permanent Secretary has asked Mrs Karen Whyte, a senior officer in the planning unit, to evaluate the system. Mrs Whyte did not design it. She plans to interview staff, review a sample of leave files and map the approval steps. The records unit holds 2,000 leave files: 1,250 from headquarters and 750 from regional offices.

c2.title: A complaints unit in St Thomas
c2.text: A municipal corporation in St Thomas has a complaints unit. Last year it spent J$7,500,000 and closed 2,500 complaints. The target is for 80% of complaints to be closed within 15 working days; 1,900 were. An evaluator, Mr Leon Campbell, sent a survey to 500 complainants and received 125 replies. One survey question reads: 'Surely you agree our staff were polite and helpful?'

c3.title: A registration system at a training centre
c3.text: A vocational training centre in Montego Bay introduced a new online registration system. Before it, the average time to register a trainee was 40 days; after it, 32 days. Of 200 registration files checked, 16 contained errors. The system cost J$6,000,000 to introduce and is expected to save J$2,000,000 a year in staff time. The principal, Mrs Jennifer Hall, asks an evaluator to report.

c4.title: A water-bill payment system
c4.text: A statutory body in the Corporate Area asked an evaluator, Ms Dorothy Grant, to review its bill-payment system. She found that 22% of customer payments are wrongly recorded and a third of the complaints concern receipts. The director, who designed the system, asks her to leave out the figure on wrongly recorded payments and to 'play down' the receipt problem. Staff interviewed were promised confidentiality; Ms Grant plans to write her report and present to the board.

c5.title: An agricultural advisory request system
c5.text: An agricultural agency in Manchester has an online system for farmers to request advice visits. Younger farmers use it easily, but many older farmers in rural districts have no internet access and phone the office instead, where calls often go unanswered. The system was paid for by a project that ends next March. The agency's manager, Mr Raymond Davis, wants an evaluation that looks at whether the system really serves farmers.

questions.q: What should Mrs Whyte do first in planning the evaluation?
o: Define the scope, aims and boundaries of the evaluation
Order new software to replace the paper system quickly
Send a survey to all 1,200 staff in the first week
Start by reviewing the files from the regional offices only
questions.why: Scope and boundaries set what is in and out, so that everything else (questions, methods, timeline) fits. Without them an evaluation drifts.

questions.q: Which people should the evaluation identify as stakeholders?
o: Only the Permanent Secretary, who asked for the evaluation to be done
Leave applicants, supervisors, HR, finance and senior managers
Only the HR officers, who keep the leave records from day to day
Only the staff who have complained about their leave balances
questions.why: Stakeholders include everyone affected by the system or interested in the findings, so that the views of users and staff are heard.

questions.q: Of the 2,000 leave files, 1,250 are from headquarters and 750 from regional offices. A proportional sample of 80 files should include how many regional files?
questions.why: 750 ÷ 2,000 = 37.5%, and 37.5% of 80 = 30 regional files, with the other 50 from headquarters.

questions.q: Mrs Whyte wants to know where delays occur between a leave request and its approval. Which tool helps most?
o: A survey asking staff how satisfied they are with the system overall
A benchmark against the leave rules used by another organisation
A Gantt chart showing the timetable of her own evaluation tasks
A process map of each step and handover, with waiting times
questions.why: A process map shows each step, and measuring the waiting time at each shows where files stop. A satisfaction survey would not locate the delay.

questions.q: The target was to close 80% of the 2,500 complaints within 15 days. 1,900 were closed in that time. What is the result?
o: 76%, so the target was missed
76%, so the target was met
80%, so the target was met
24%, so the target was missed
questions.why: 1,900 ÷ 2,500 = 0.76, or 76%. The target was 80%, so it was missed, by 4 percentage points (100 complaints).

questions.q: What was the cost per complaint closed in the complaints unit last year?
What was the response rate to the survey?
questions.why: 125 ÷ 500 = 0.25, or 25%. A quarter of the people asked replied, so the report should say how far the results can be relied on.

questions.q: The survey asks, 'Surely you agree our staff were polite and helpful?' What is wrong with it?
o: It is too long and detailed for respondents to answer quickly
It asks about two different services in the same single question
It cannot be answered because it offers no rating scale to use
It is a leading question that pushes respondents to agree
questions.why: A question that suggests the expected answer produces biased results. A neutral wording, such as 'How would you rate our staff?', is better.

questions.q: The average registration time hides differences between cases. What else should the evaluator look at?
o: The longest and shortest times, and types of registration
The average time for other training centres in other parishes
Only the registrations completed by the most experienced clerks
The time that registration took before the college first opened
questions.why: An average can hide a few very slow cases. Looking at the range and at types of case shows whether the improvement is real for everyone.

questions.q: Of 200 files checked, 16 contained errors. What is the error rate?
questions.why: 16 ÷ 200 = 0.08, or 8%. The evaluator should also say whether the files were chosen at random.

questions.q: How should the evaluator check the expected saving of J$2,000,000 a year?
o: Accept the supplier's estimate, since the supplier knows the system best
Ask staff how much time they believe they now save each week
Compare staff hours and overtime records before and after the system
Use the saving expected by the college for the next annual budget
questions.why: An expected saving is a claim to be tested. Records from before and after the change, the baseline and the new figures, give evidence that does not depend on opinion.

questions.q: Which comparison best shows the effect of the new registration system?
o: Registration time now, compared with that of a much larger college
Opinions of the staff who introduced it, collected only last week
The cost of the system compared with the whole training budget
Registration time and errors now, against the baseline before it
questions.why: Only a before-and-after comparison with the baseline, using the same measures, shows whether things changed. Without a baseline you cannot say whether it improved.

questions.q: The director, who designed the system, asks Ms Grant to leave out the 22% figure and 'play down' the receipt problem. What should she do?
o: Keep the finding and offer to discuss the evidence with him
Remove it, because he knows the system better than she does
Keep it but replace the figure with a vague phrase such as 'a few'
Remove it from the written report and give it to the board orally
questions.why: A finding supported by evidence must stay in the report. The evaluator can discuss the evidence, correct real errors and use fair wording, but cannot suppress it.

questions.q: Ms Grant wants to check the finding that 22% of payments are wrongly recorded. What is the best step?
o: Repeat the same count of the same files at the end of the week
Compare a sample of payments with bank records and receipts
Ask the director whether he believes the figure is right or wrong
Ask three customers whether they think the figure is too high
questions.why: Triangulation checks a finding against independent sources. Bank records and receipts test the figure; opinions and a repeated count of the same data do not.

questions.q: A junior clerk is nervous and asks whether she must take part in an interview. What should Ms Grant say?
o: Everyone in the unit must take part, as the director has already agreed to it
She may decline, but then her refusal will be reported to her supervisor
Taking part is voluntary, and her comments will not be linked to her name
She should take part, because the report needs the views of all staff
questions.why: Evaluation should rest on informed, voluntary participation. Explaining purpose and confidentiality builds trust and honest answers.

questions.q: Ms Grant wants to set out the possible causes of the wrong receipts, grouped under staff, procedures, the IT system and forms. Which tool suits this best?
o: A line chart of monthly payment totals
A Gantt chart of the evaluation timetable
A pie chart of complaints by parish
A fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram
questions.why: A fishbone diagram has the problem at its head and groups possible causes on its bones, so that each can be tested against the data.

questions.q: Many older farmers cannot use the online system. Which criterion does this raise most?
o: Equity
Economy
Efficiency
Sustainability
questions.why: Equity asks whether all groups are served fairly. A system that excludes older, rural farmers fails on equity, even if it is quick for others.

questions.q: The agency has found that most farmers now ask for advice by mobile phone call or WhatsApp message. Which criterion does this raise most?
o: Economy
Relevance
Effectiveness
Sustainability
questions.why: Relevance asks whether the system's design still matches the needs of its users. An online-only form may no longer fit how farmers actually ask for help.

questions.q: The evaluator wants to understand why older farmers do not use the system. Which method is best?
o: A survey sent by email to all farmers who are on the system
A review of the system log-ins over the past six months
Interviews and a focus group with older farmers
An analysis of the cost of each advice visit to farmers
questions.why: Reasons are best explored by talking with people. An email survey would miss those who are offline, and log-ins show only who used the system.

questions.q: Which element of a logic model for the advisory system is an outcome rather than an output?
o: The number of advice visits that were carried out last year
The number of requests that were received online each month
The number of extension officers employed by the agency
Farmers who report better yields after the advice visit
questions.why: An outcome is a change that results for users. Counts of visits, requests or staff are outputs or inputs.
